THOUGHT: The patient is a 2-year-old girl with progressive irritability, episodic pallor and cyanosis (i.e., “tet spells”), and a known but previously uninvestigated heart murmur. Her physical exam reveals a characteristic squatting posture when distressed — a compensatory maneuver in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) that increases systemic vascular resistance, thereby reducing right-to-left shunting and improving oxygenation. The harsh systolic ejection murmur at the upper left sternal border is consistent with pulmonary stenosis, a key component of TOF. The chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart — a classic radiographic sign reflecting right ventricular hypertrophy and decreased pulmonary vascular markings (though lung fields are described as “clear,” which in this context likely means no pulmonary congestion or infiltrates, compatible with decreased pulmonary blood flow). Crucially, the echocardiogram definitively demonstrates the four cardinal features of TOF: ventricular septal defect (VSD), pulmonary stenosis (infundibular and/or valvular), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. No other congenital lesion explains this constellation of clinical, physical, radiographic, and echocardiographic findings.

DIAGNOSIS: Tetralogy of Fallot
